title: Vase with Butterflies
medium: Porcelain with cobalt blue, pink, and white under transparent glaze

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Charles Stewart Smith, 1893
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A porcelain vase from Japan decorated with butterflies. The decoration uses cobalt blue, pink, and white beneath a clear glaze.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag, credit line, classification (Ceramics), culture (Japan), tag (Butterflies), and image URLs read from the record

context: A porcelain vase credited to the Japanese potter Katō Tomotarō and dated by the Met to the late 19th century. The Met's medium line says the colors cobalt blue, pink, and white lie under a transparent glaze, and the butterflies are named in the title.

descriptions.k: This is a vase made of porcelain in Japan. Butterflies decorate it! The colors are blue, pink, and white. Can you find the butterflies? How many wings can you count? Would you put flowers in this vase?
descriptions.g12: A potter in Japan made this porcelain vase long ago. Butterflies are painted on it in blue, pink, and white. A clear glaze covers the colors, so the vase looks smooth and shiny. Where do you see the butterflies? How do the colors work together on the round vase?
descriptions.g35: Katō Tomotarō, a Japanese potter, is credited with this porcelain vase from the late 1800s. Butterflies decorate it in cobalt blue, pink, and white under a clear glaze, which means the colors were painted before the glaze was added and fired. Look at how the butterflies wrap around the curved surface. Why might an artist choose butterflies to decorate a vase?
descriptions.g68: This vase combines a useful object with delicate decoration. The Met's record says the cobalt blue, pink, and white colors lie under a transparent glaze, which protects the design and gives the surface a glassy shine. Butterflies are a popular subject in Japanese art and may suggest the lightness of spring, though meanings vary. Notice how the artist fits flying insects onto a curved surface. How does the vase's shape change how you view the design?
descriptions.g910: Katō Tomotarō's Vase with Butterflies uses underglaze color on porcelain, so the decoration sits beneath a transparent glaze rather than on top of it. The curved form of the vase and the scattered butterflies invite you to move around it, seeing the design unfold. In Japanese art, butterflies appear in many contexts and can carry different associations, so a single reading would be uncertain. Consider how technique, shape, and motif combine to turn a utilitarian form into a display piece.
descriptions.g1112: As a late 19th-century Japanese porcelain with underglaze decoration, Vase with Butterflies belongs to a period when Japanese ceramics were widely exhibited and collected abroad, which helps explain its presence in a Western museum. The butterfly motif carries varied associations in East Asian visual culture, but the record offers no text to anchor one. Underglaze technique matters here: color applied before glazing and firing resists wear and gains depth. What can the form, surface, and motif support, and what must remain open?

teacherNote.context: A late 19th-century Japanese porcelain vase with butterflies, credited to Katō Tomotarō. The Met records its colors as cobalt blue, pink, and white under a transparent glaze.
directions: Have students design a repeating butterfly pattern for a curved surface, such as a paper cup, and discuss how curvature changes the design.
Discuss why painting under a glaze helps protect a design.
Compare how this vase and another ceramic in the archive combine function with decoration.
